hard_spots.why_hard: シチュエイション, バック/ハイケイ, ゲンジツシュギ, グタイ/クウタイ arrive as sound. Nekohachi guesses situation is a fix he is trapped in and compromise is flattery; he hears background as pure noise and thinks of konnyaku mondō. Translating them into smooth English criticism erases the joke and his truer misuse.
He keeps asking a novel for an ochi/conclusion as if it were rakugo. The group laughs at the wrong place. English must keep punchline/fall without explaining rakugo or making him knowing.

Half the night is second-hand Kume retold by the host, interrupted and judged thin. Polishing it into a moving tale betrays its flat reported texture and makes Nekohachi's recognition look disproportionate.
Nightingale, valley-crossing, crickets, cranes, frogs (くッくッ, かッかッ, けきょ), earthworm vs mole-cricket lore. They must read as act, with the room's thin laughter left thin, not as nature writing.
○○○様, ○○家, ○○子爵 are in the source as discretion about lords. Filling them, footnoting guesses, or smoothing to a certain lord removes the performed knowing-how-to-behave.

Tao Yuanming's return, Sanba as praise, konnyaku mondō as cover for not understanding. Each is Nekohachi dignifying incomprehension or the wish to leave; footnotes must be minimal and never award him the point.

でげす, な, beranmei, 大山大将, Kōdan Club, Sugamo madhouse, Yoshiwara embankment, rickety suburban allotment, petitioned gas lamp. Requires dropped run-on colloquial syntax without Cockney or stage-Japanese, and inventory without lyricism.

narration.english_tense: Past as default for narrated action and interior slide; keep present only where Japanese stage directions or gnomic asides demand it. Do not hop tenses to manufacture climax at p175 or p185.
narration.frame: One evening's drift: tram ride home from two engagements, two-hour writers' meeting, midnight walk to a suburban row-house gate. Flash memories (candy-selling, frog discovery, lord visits) surface inside that drift without chapter breaks beyond the seven numbered cuts.
narration.narrator: Close third person glued to Nekohachi; slides into his idiom, jokes and self-justifications without endorsing or correcting them. Even at the most abject admissions (wife-beating, fee-shame) the tone stays dogged and garrulous.
narration.person: third person, internally focalised on Nekohachi
narration.tense_habits: Japanese moves freely between past recollection, present-tense stagey aside, and gnomic summary; subjects drop for stretches and speakers go unattributed. English must tolerate long associative sentences and delayed attribution rather than rationalising them.

part_summaries.summary: 一. On the tram home reading Kōdan Club, Nekohachi is hailed by patron Takami. Passengers become an audience; he answers a Sugamo joke with a madmen-and-monsters quip, swallows a fat joke, then drifts into comedian's苦労, protecting his voice by not drinking, and allotment pests including night-working cutworms. Takami invites him to a writers' study group; worried about seedlings, he follows, rheumatic and limping.

二. They enter a house with a cucumber plot and climb to six or seven writers. Introduced as the famous Nekohachi, he charms and apologises for rheumatism. The host, a bathhouse acquaintance, begins the absent T-kun's agenda item: Kume's Tiger from May Bunsho Sekai. The paraphrase of a comic actor given only a beast's part hits Nekohachi as his own life with four sons and a gifted twelve-year-old he keeps from the yose.

三. The paraphrase continues through zoo research, a sharp critic, applause for a yawn and leap. Nekohachi misuses situation to protest the compromise and is ignored. The ending is told: after the ovation the costumed father finds his small son weeping in the dark wings and tiger and human child weep together. Nekohachi, half-performing grief, objects that Fukai should never have let the child see it and tells of hiding his own sons in the suburbs.

四. The group calls Tiger thin and backgroundless. The Tenjin-like man reveals Kume himself wrote the savage anonymous Jiji Shinpō review; Nekohachi takes Kume for a Sanba-like wit and says the audience decides. A silent student asks about personality backing work; host and others answer with concrete/abstract jargon Nekohachi hears as konnyaku mondō. Talk drifts; hostess gives him cakes and children's magazines; Takami calls for a performance.

五. Triumphant in his own world, he does caged and valley nightingales, crickets, crows, mole-crickets, cranes, and earthworm lore that once got him taken for a burglar. Asked for his motive, he tells the candy-seller origin: rheumatism, failed peddling, frog sexes distinguished on the Yoshiwara bank, then sales. Warned against vulgarisation, he defends fooling audiences, mimics a cat fight, and tells failed upper-house visits with borrowed kimono and blanked lordly names.

六. Three including the near-sighted man leave mid-story; Nekohachi resents it as true rudeness. Fee pride is debated: he will not name a price yet will go free if moved. Pig-farming talk excludes him; hungry and bored, he frets over who pays, talks gardens with the hostess to cover his face, and eats more cakes.

七. Near 1 a.m. by the waste-hospital forest they disperse. Pockets stuffed with old magazines and cake leavings as fee, he wants to embrace the tiger and weep. Takami quietly slips him two yen; ashamed of relief and wanting to quit, he sees them off, advertises cucumbers and eggplants at his dark gate, and goes to his door past sleeping rows to retell the novel to his wife.

data.say: Keep Nekohachi's working patter and the writers' borrowed abstractions as two unblended Englishes; keep the Tiger paraphrase flat and the garden inventory serious; let his borrowed sorrow stay learned, performed and real at once without resolving him into victim or butt.

style_sheet.annotation_density: Sparse. Annotate only what the sentence cannot give: yose/kōza, Kōdan Club, Sugamo madhouse, shinpa, Tao Yuanming, Sanba, konnyaku mondō if kept. Never gloss what context supplies or explain his misunderstandings in-text.
style_sheet.author_voice: Taishō naturalist inventory: dogged, repetitive, faintly garrulous even when sad; long associative slides; lists of food, pests, coins, cries. Do not lyricise the sad passages or brisk up the comic ones; the bathos at p175 and the rare humility at p185 must read at the same temperature as the tram jokes.
style_sheet.honorifics_and_names: Japanese order surname-first for Japanese names. Keep Sensei for Nekohachi's address to Takami and others because the relation lives in it; keep -san/-kun/-sama where socially load-bearing (Takami-san, Nekohachi-san/Kun, Tenjin-sama as nickname). Romanise with macrons: Nekohachi, Takami, Kume, Tō Enmei, Fukai.
style_sheet.keep_in_japanese: Keep Sensei, yose, kōza, and the English-derived loanwords as situation/background where the joke is mouthing English; keep ochi as fall/punchline glossed once if needed. Keep blanked names as blanks (Mr ___, the ___ house) not filled.
style_sheet.quotation: Use single quotes for quoted Tiger paraphrase inside host speech where needed; double quotes for direct speech. Keep the group's thin laughter as ha, ha, ha without upgrading to roars.
style_sheet.register: Two audible Englishes, never merged: Nekohachi in dropped, run-on, self-interrupting colloquial patter with verbal tics for な/でげす, competent about gardens and mimicry; writers in flat borrowed critical abstraction. Neither polished into the same literary fluency.
style_sheet.ruby_and_italics: No ruby in English. Italicise only loanwords kept as Japanese and titles of works/magazines (Tiger, Bunso Sekai, Kōdan Club) on first use; otherwise roman.
